results.summary: Silicon Strummer turns a VGA monitor into a playable guitar fretboard with an 8x6 grid of notes. The user moves a cursor with four buttons and holds a fifth button to output a square wave tone at the selected note's frequency. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for display and a speaker or audio circuit on uio[7] for sound. The design is a simple educational music toy that fits in a single tile and can also be tested in the Tiny Tapeout VGA Playground.

This project is a 16x16 digital compute-in-memory (DCIM) core implemented in Verilog for an experimental IHP SG13G2 CMOS5L shuttle. It provides an array that can be written to and executed, with results read out via dedicated pins. The documentation is essentially a placeholder, stating only that it is a DCIM core and that testing details are in progress. No external hardware or usage instructions are provided, so its practical application and interface remain unclear.

This project is an 8x8 digital compute-in-memory (DCIM) core implemented in Verilog for an experimental IHP SG13G2 CMOS5L shuttle. It provides an array that can be written to and executed, with results read out via dedicated pins. The documentation is essentially a placeholder, stating only that it is a DCIM core and that testing details are in progress. No external hardware or usage instructions are provided, so its practical application and interface remain unclear.

Orion Iron Ion is a demo competition entry that generates a 640x480 VGA video with a logo, star field, floating-point twister, and spiralling balls, accompanied by a synthesizer and sequencer. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and Mike's audio PMOD for sound, and runs directly after reset with all inputs set to zero. The design is clocked at 50.4 MHz, giving two clock cycles per pixel. It is a showcase of real-time graphics and audio on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

Cat VGA is a bouncing cat screensaver for VGA output, currently implemented in Verilog. The author plans to add an SPI interface for time and an encrypted key so the ASIC can decrypt and reply with a TOTP code. No hardware has been built yet, and the documentation is minimal. The design is a work in progress and may change into a different project.

This project implements an 8-bit CPU in Verilog that performs arithmetic and load instructions and outputs the result of each instruction. It is designed to work with an external microcontroller that acts as an instruction register, providing program counter values and returning instructions. A test script simulates the instruction register to allow custom assembly code to be run and tested. The documentation describes the goal and testing approach but does not provide detailed schematics or a complete instruction set.

serdes8b10 is a test design for an 8b10b serializer/deserializer, containing an encoder and decoder that can push 9-bit symbols and pop results after a number of clocks. It requires a manual clock divided by 10 to generate internal clocks, and uses bidirectional pins for data, strobes, and clock outputs. The testing procedure involves sending a COM character to lock the link and then verifying that transmitted characters are received correctly. The documentation provides detailed pin-level instructions but notes that formal test documentation is still to be added.

The Titan Processing Unit (TPU) is a 16-bit computer based on the Nand2Tetris Hack architecture, which fetches instructions via SPI from an off-chip memory module. The memory module, simulated on an RP2040, stores ROM and RAM partitions, and programs are loaded into the RP2040's ROM section. The CPU executes the fetched instructions and provides general-purpose I/O. The design is a working implementation of the Hack computer with modifications for physical feasibility, and it requires an external SPI RAM module for operation.

Space-Time Waves and Filaments is a purely combinatorial generative video synthesizer that produces continuously evolving procedural art on a 640x480 VGA display at 60Hz. It uses bitwise operations and triangle waves instead of RAM or DSP blocks, and offers six selectable visual engines controlled by input pins. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD or compatible DAC and a VGA monitor, plus switches or buttons to change modes. It is notable for fitting complex mathematical patterns into a single tile through a targeted 'math diet' that reduces logic gate count.

Tiny Blackjack is a simplified Blackjack game implemented entirely in digital hardware, with game logic as a finite-state machine and a 16-bit LFSR for pseudo-random card generation. The player uses four buttons (Hit, Stand, Double, Start/Deal) to interact, and the game state is displayed on a VGA screen showing cards and balance. It requires a VGA module and four push-buttons connected to the specified input pins. The design fits into a single TinyTapeout tile and includes features like doubling down and real-time hand total calculation.
